prompt: Which of these statements about approximation schemes are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Knapsack has an FPTAS: it supports any chosen positive relative-error tolerance, with time polynomial in the input length and the inverse tolerance
options.explanation: Correct. Round item values while controlling the total loss, then run the pseudo-polynomial dynamic program on those smaller values.
It's APX-hard: approximating below 123/122 is NP-hard, so no PTAS exists unless P equals NP. (Euclidean TSP, a special case, does have one: Arora, 1998.)

options.text: A strongly NP-hard problem with polynomially bounded nonnegative integer objective values has no FPTAS unless P equals NP
options.explanation: Correct. Choose ε smaller than one over the largest possible objective value; the FPTAS's error is then less than 1, so on integers it must return the exact optimum in polynomial time.

options.text: An FPTAS returns the exact optimum in polynomial time
options.explanation: No: it returns a solution within a chosen relative error ε of optimal, with running time growing polynomially in one over ε.
Vertex cover is APX-hard (NP-hard to approximate below about 1.414), so it has no PTAS unless P equals NP.

workedExample: A PTAS is polynomial for each fixed accuracy; an FPTAS is also polynomial in inverse accuracy. Knapsack achieves the latter by rounding values while controlling total loss. For a hard family with polynomially bounded integer objectives, an FPTAS could make the absolute error smaller than one in polynomial time, forcing the exact optimum. That would contradict the stated hardness unless P equals NP.
